title: Cleaning Data
description: The essential cleanup skills: handling missing values thoughtfully, spotting outliers, removing duplicates, and fixing data type problems.

lessons.title: Handling Missing Values
lessons.description: Learn how to find missing data, understand why it's missing, and decide what to do about it.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can detect missing values in a dataset and choose an appropriate strategy for handling them.

sections.title: 🔎 Finding missing values
sections.content:
Pandas represents missing data as `NaN` (Not a Number). Find it with `.isna()`.

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"age": [25, None, 42], "city": ["Lahore", "Karachi", None]})

print(df.isna().sum())
# age     1
# city    1
# dtype: int64
```

`.isna().sum()` is one of the fastest ways to get a per-column count of how much data is missing.

sections.title: 🤔 Why is it missing? (This matters more than how)
sections.content:
Before deciding what to do, ask *why* the data is missing:

• **Missing completely at random** — a sensor glitch, no pattern (safest to fill or drop)
• **Missing for a reason related to the data itself** — customers who didn't buy anything might have no "last purchase date" *because* they never purchased — that absence is informative, not noise!

Treating meaningful absence the same as random noise throws away a real signal.

sections.title: 🛠️ Common strategies
sections.content:
There's no single correct answer — it depends on the situation:

```python
# Drop rows with any missing values
df.dropna()

# Fill with a specific value
df["age"].fillna(0)

# Fill with the column's mean (common for numeric data)
df["age"].fillna(df["age"].mean())

# Add a flag column marking where data was missing, before filling it
df["age_was_missing"] = df["age"].isna()
df["age"] = df["age"].fillna(df["age"].mean())
```

• Dropping loses information — fine if missingness is rare and random
• Filling with the mean/median keeps the row but can understate spread
• A missing-indicator flag preserves the *fact* that something was missing, even after filling

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Filling missing values before asking why they're missing.** If absence is meaningful, filling it in erases a real signal.

**Dropping large amounts of data without checking how much you're losing.** `.dropna()` on a dataset where 40% of rows have some missing value can throw away most of your data.

**Filling with the mean/median without adding a missingness flag when it might matter.** You lose the information that the value was originally unknown.

questions.question: What does `df.isna().sum()` show you?
options: The total number of rows in the DataFrame
The count of missing values per column
The mean of every numeric column
Whether the DataFrame is empty
questions.explanation: `.isna()` produces a True/False grid where True marks missing values, and `.sum()` adds those up per column, giving a missing-value count for each.

questions.question: Why might a missing "last purchase date" be meaningful rather than random?
options: It's always a data entry error
It could indicate the customer never made a purchase — the absence itself is informative
Missing dates are always safe to fill with today's date
There's no way missing data can be meaningful
questions.explanation: Sometimes missingness itself carries a signal — here, a blank field might mean "this event never happened," which is very different from a random data gap.

questions.question: What's the benefit of adding a missing-indicator flag before filling in a value?
options: It speeds up the fillna() operation
It preserves the information that a value was originally unknown, even after it's filled in
It removes the need to fill missing values at all
It automatically fixes data entry errors
questions.explanation: Filling a missing value with the mean makes the row usable, but it erases the fact that the value was unknown — an indicator column keeps that information available to a later model or analysis.

questions.question: What does `df['col'].fillna(0)` do?
options: Deletes all rows with missing values in that column
Replaces missing values in that column with 0
Removes the column entirely
Counts how many values are missing
questions.explanation: fillna() replaces missing (NaN) entries with a specified value — here, filling gaps in the column with 0.

questions.question: What's a risk of using `dropna()` too aggressively?
options: It's always completely safe with no downside
It can discard a large portion of your dataset if many rows have at least one missing value somewhere
dropna() only removes columns, never rows
It automatically fixes the underlying data quality issue
questions.explanation: If missing values are scattered across many columns, dropping every row with any missing value can throw away far more data than necessary.

questions.question: What are the three broad strategies for handling missing values mentioned as common approaches?
options: Ignore, hide, and rename
Drop the rows/columns, impute a value, or flag that it was missing
Convert everything to text
Always fill with zero
questions.explanation: Common strategies include dropping incomplete rows or columns, imputing a reasonable substitute value, or adding a flag noting the value was originally missing.

questions.question: Why might you choose the median over the mean when imputing a missing numeric value?
options: The median is always required by pandas
The median is less sensitive to outliers, so it can give a more representative fill value for skewed data
The mean can't be computed if any value is missing
There's no meaningful difference between them
questions.explanation: Because extreme outliers pull the mean away from the 'typical' value, the median often gives a more robust and representative choice for imputation in skewed data.

questions.question: Why is it useful to check the percentage of missing values per column, not just the raw count?
options: Raw counts are always more informative than percentages
A percentage puts the missingness in context — 50 missing values means something very different in a 100-row dataset versus a 1,000,000-row dataset
Percentages can't be computed for missing data
It's not useful — only totals matter
questions.explanation: A count alone doesn't reveal severity — the same number of missing values represents a minor issue in a huge dataset but a major one in a small one, which the percentage makes clear.

lessons.title: Finding and Handling Outliers
lessons.description: Learn how to spot unusually extreme values and decide whether they're errors or real signal.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can identify outliers using summary statistics and explain the tradeoffs in different ways of handling them.

sections.title: 🎯 What counts as an outlier?
sections.content:
An **outlier** is a value that's unusually far from the rest of the data. Outliers aren't automatically "wrong" — sometimes they're the most important rows in the dataset (like a fraudulent transaction, or a record-breaking sale).

The key question isn't just "is this extreme?" but "is this extreme value an error, or a real, important observation?"

sections.title: 📏 A common way to detect them: IQR
sections.content:
The **interquartile range (IQR)** method flags values far outside the "typical" middle range of the data.

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"price": [10, 12, 11, 13, 9, 500]})

q1 = df["price"].quantile(0.25)
q3 = df["price"].quantile(0.75)
iqr = q3 - q1

lower = q1 - 1.5 * iqr
upper = q3 + 1.5 * iqr

outliers = df[(df["price"] < lower) | (df["price"] > upper)]
print(outliers)   # flags the 500
```

1.5×IQR beyond the 25th/75th percentile is a common, if somewhat arbitrary, rule of thumb.

sections.title: ⚖️ Deciding what to do
sections.content:
Once flagged, you have a few options, and the right one depends on *why* the outlier exists:

• **It's a data entry error** (age = 999) → fix or drop it
• **It's real but you want to reduce its influence** → cap it at a reasonable maximum (called **winsorizing**)
• **It's the exact thing you're trying to detect** (fraud, a rare disease) → keep it, and make sure your analysis doesn't accidentally throw it away

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Automatically deleting every flagged outlier.** Some outliers are the most valuable rows in the dataset — always investigate before deleting.

**Using the mean to check for outliers.** The mean itself gets pulled by outliers — the IQR method (based on the median-adjacent quartiles) is more robust.

**Applying the same outlier rule to every column blindly.** A reasonable range for "age" is very different from a reasonable range for "annual revenue" — think about each column's real-world meaning.

questions.question: Why shouldn't outliers automatically be deleted from a dataset?
options: Outliers are always data entry errors
Some outliers represent the exact phenomenon you're trying to study, like fraud or rare events
Deleting rows is technically impossible in pandas
Outliers never affect analysis results
questions.explanation: An outlier might be a genuine, important observation (like a fraudulent transaction) rather than an error — deleting it without investigating could throw away the most important data point.

questions.question: What does the IQR outlier method use as its reference range?
options: The full range from minimum to maximum
The spread between the 25th and 75th percentiles
Only the mean and standard deviation
The first and last rows of the dataset
questions.explanation: IQR (interquartile range) is Q3 minus Q1 — the spread of the middle 50% of the data — and typical outlier bounds extend 1.5×IQR beyond Q1 and Q3.

questions.question: What does "winsorizing" a value mean?
options: Deleting the row entirely
Capping an extreme value at a reasonable maximum or minimum instead of removing it
Converting the value to a missing value
Rounding the value to the nearest integer
questions.explanation: Winsorizing keeps the row but limits how extreme its value can be, reducing the outlier's influence while preserving the rest of the row's information.

questions.question: Besides IQR, what's another common way to detect outliers?
options: Counting the number of columns
Using a z-score threshold, flagging values many standard deviations from the mean
Sorting the data alphabetically
Checking the file size
questions.explanation: The z-score method flags values based on how many standard deviations they are from the mean, offering a different way to catch extreme points than IQR.

questions.question: What's the difference between an outlier caused by a data entry error and a legitimate extreme value?
options: There's no meaningful difference — treat them identically
An entry error is a mistake to fix or remove, while a legitimate extreme value is a real, valid observation worth investigating rather than discarding
Legitimate extreme values never occur in real datasets
Entry errors are always larger than legitimate extremes
questions.explanation: A typo like an age of 200 is a data quality issue to fix, but a genuinely enormous but real transaction amount is valid information that shouldn't be casually discarded.

questions.question: How can a box plot help with outlier detection?
options: It cannot be used for that purpose
Points plotted beyond the whiskers visually highlight potential outliers based on the IQR range
It only shows the mean value
It requires the data to have no missing values first
questions.explanation: A box plot visually marks points outside the whisker range (typically based on IQR) as individual dots, making outliers easy to spot at a glance.

questions.question: Why does domain knowledge matter when deciding what to do with an outlier?
options: Domain knowledge is irrelevant to statistical decisions
Only someone familiar with the data's context can judge whether an extreme value is a real event worth keeping or a data problem worth fixing
Outlier decisions should always be made purely by statistical formulas
Domain knowledge only matters for categorical columns
questions.explanation: Statistics alone can flag a value as unusual, but understanding the real-world context is what tells you whether it's meaningful signal or a mistake.

questions.question: What's the tradeoff between capping (winsorizing) an outlier versus removing it entirely?
options: There is no tradeoff — capping is always strictly better
Capping keeps the row (and its other column values) while reducing the extreme value's influence, whereas removing the row discards all of its information
Removing a row always preserves more information than capping
Capping can only be applied to categorical data
questions.explanation: Capping lets you retain the rest of that row's data while limiting the extreme value's distortion, while outright removal loses everything else in that row too.

lessons.title: Duplicates and Data Consistency
lessons.description: Learn how to catch duplicate records and inconsistent category labels before they distort your analysis.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can detect and remove duplicate rows and standardize inconsistent category values.

sections.title: 👯 Finding duplicate rows
sections.content:
Duplicate rows can sneak in from double data entry, merging datasets, or a buggy data pipeline.

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Ana", "Bo", "Ana"],
    "age": [25, 31, 25],
})

print(df.duplicated())        # [False, False, True]
print(df.duplicated().sum())  # 1

df_clean = df.drop_duplicates()
```

By default, `.duplicated()` flags a row as a duplicate only if *every* column matches an earlier row exactly.

sections.title: 🎯 Duplicates on a subset of columns
sections.content:
Sometimes "duplicate" means something narrower — like two rows sharing the same customer ID, even if other columns differ (perhaps due to an update).

```python
# Consider rows duplicates if they share the same customer_id,
# and keep only the most recent one
df.drop_duplicates(subset="customer_id", keep="last")
```

sections.title: 🔤 Inconsistent category labels
sections.content:
The same category is often written multiple inconsistent ways: "USA", "U.S.A.", "United States", "usa". Pandas treats each spelling as a *different* category unless you clean it up.

```python
df["country"] = df["country"].str.strip().str.lower()
df["country"] = df["country"].replace({
    "usa": "united states",
    "u.s.a.": "united states",
})
```

Always check `.value_counts()` on categorical columns early — it's the fastest way to spot messy, inconsistent labels.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Not checking `.value_counts()` on category columns before analyzing.** Inconsistent labels silently split what should be one group into several smaller ones.

**Removing duplicates without deciding which one to keep.** If duplicate rows differ slightly (like an updated address), `keep="first"` vs `keep="last"` gives very different results.

**Assuming `.duplicated()` catches near-duplicates.** It only flags exact matches — a typo like "Lahroe" instead of "Lahore" won't be caught automatically.

questions.question: By default, when does `.duplicated()` flag a row as a duplicate?
options: When any single column matches an earlier row
When every column exactly matches an earlier row
When the row is the first occurrence of its values
It never flags anything by default
questions.explanation: By default, pandas considers a row a duplicate of an earlier one only when all columns match exactly — you can narrow this with the `subset` parameter.

questions.question: Why is `.value_counts()` useful on a categorical column?
options: It computes the mean of the column
It quickly reveals inconsistent labels, like "USA" and "usa" being counted as separate categories
It removes missing values automatically
It only works on numeric columns
questions.explanation: `.value_counts()` shows every distinct value and its frequency, making it easy to spot when the same real-world category is split across multiple inconsistent spellings.

questions.question: What's the risk of blindly running `drop_duplicates()` without deciding which duplicate to keep?
options: There is no risk — it always keeps the correct row
If duplicate rows have slightly different values (like an updated field), you might keep outdated or wrong information
It deletes the entire DataFrame
It only works on numeric columns
questions.explanation: When "duplicate" rows aren't perfectly identical (e.g. one has an updated address), which one `drop_duplicates()` keeps by default matters — worth checking `keep="first"` vs `keep="last"` deliberately.

questions.question: What does passing `subset=['email']` to `.duplicated()` do?
options: It ignores the email column entirely
It flags rows as duplicates based only on matching email values, ignoring other columns
It deletes the email column
It has no effect — subset is not a valid parameter
questions.explanation: The subset parameter restricts the duplicate check to specific columns, so rows are flagged as duplicates if just those columns match, regardless of the rest.

questions.question: How would you standardize inconsistent capitalization in a category column, like 'USA' vs 'usa'?
options: df['col'] = df['col'].str.lower()
df['col'].capitalize_all()
This can't be fixed programmatically
df.fix_case('col')
questions.explanation: Applying `.str.lower()` (or `.str.upper()`) normalizes the casing across all values, so variants that should match actually do.

questions.question: What does the `keep` parameter in `drop_duplicates()` control?
options: Whether to keep the DataFrame in memory
Which of the duplicate rows to retain — the first occurrence, the last, or none of them
Whether duplicates are counted or removed
It has no effect on drop_duplicates()
questions.explanation: `keep='first'`, `keep='last'`, or `keep=False` determines which duplicate row (if any) survives when duplicates are removed.

questions.question: What's a common, easy-to-miss source of near-duplicate rows?
options: Rows with different numeric values
Extra whitespace or inconsistent formatting in text fields, making values look different even though they represent the same thing
Rows with no missing values
Rows sorted in a different order
questions.explanation: Trailing spaces, inconsistent capitalization, or slightly different formatting can make two rows that represent the same real-world thing appear as distinct values to pandas.

questions.question: Why should deduplication typically happen before aggregation (like groupby)?
options: Deduplication always happens automatically during aggregation
Duplicate rows would otherwise be counted multiple times, inflating sums, counts, and averages
Order doesn't matter — the results are always identical either way
Aggregation functions ignore duplicate rows automatically
questions.explanation: If duplicates remain when you sum or average, each duplicated row contributes extra weight to the result, skewing the aggregation.

lessons.title: Data Type Conversion Pitfalls
lessons.description: Learn the common ways data types quietly go wrong, and how to fix them safely.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can convert columns to the correct data type and recognize common conversion pitfalls.

sections.title: 🔄 Converting types with astype and to_numeric
sections.content:
```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"price": ["10", "20", "30"]})

df["price"] = df["price"].astype(float)
print(df.dtypes)  # price float64
```

For messier numeric-looking text (with stray characters), `pd.to_numeric(..., errors="coerce")` is safer — it turns anything it can't convert into `NaN` instead of crashing.

sections.title: 📅 Dates need explicit conversion too
sections.content:
Dates loaded from a file are usually plain text until you convert them.

```python
df["signup_date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["signup_date"])

# Now date-aware operations work:
df["signup_year"] = df["signup_date"].dt.year
```

Without this conversion, you can't sort dates correctly, extract the year/month, or compute date differences — pandas would just treat them as arbitrary strings.

sections.title: 💰 Currency and formatted numbers
sections.content:
Numbers formatted for humans ("$1,200.50") need cleanup before they can become numeric.

```python
df["amount"] = (
    df["amount"]
    .str.replace("$", "", regex=False)
    .str.replace(",", "", regex=False)
    .astype(float)
)
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming a column is numeric just because the values look like numbers.** If it was loaded as text, sorting and math will behave unexpectedly ("9" > "10" alphabetically!) until it's explicitly converted.

**Using `.astype()` on messy data and getting a crash.** `pd.to_numeric(..., errors="coerce")` is more forgiving when some values genuinely aren't convertible.

**Forgetting to convert dates, then trying to sort or filter by them.** Text-typed "dates" sort alphabetically, not chronologically — "2024-02-01" would sort before "2023-12-01" as plain text.

questions.question: Why would sorting a text-typed numeric column give a surprising order, like "9" appearing after "10"?
options: Pandas has a sorting bug
Text is sorted character by character (alphabetically), not by numeric value, until the column is converted to a numeric type
This never actually happens
Only string columns can be sorted
questions.explanation: As text, "10" comes before "9" alphabetically because '1' sorts before '9' character by character — converting the column to numeric fixes this by sorting on actual values.

questions.question: What advantage does `pd.to_numeric(col, errors="coerce")` have over `.astype(float)`?
options: It's faster to type
It converts unconvertible values to NaN instead of raising an error and crashing
It automatically removes missing values
There is no difference
questions.explanation: `errors="coerce"` gracefully turns values that can't be converted into NaN, letting the rest of the column convert successfully instead of the whole operation failing.

questions.question: Why do dates loaded from a CSV usually need explicit conversion with `pd.to_datetime()`?
options: CSV files can't contain dates at all
Without conversion, pandas treats them as plain text, which breaks chronological sorting and date-based calculations
It's purely optional and never causes issues
Dates are automatically detected and converted on load
questions.explanation: Dates read from a file default to text (object) type — converting with `pd.to_datetime()` unlocks correct chronological sorting, filtering, and date-part extraction like `.dt.year`.

questions.question: What's the risk of using `.astype(int)` on a column of decimal values like 4.9?
options: It rounds to the nearest integer, 5
It truncates toward zero, silently turning 4.9 into 4 rather than rounding
It raises an error for any non-integer value
It converts the value to a string instead
questions.explanation: astype(int) truncates rather than rounds, so 4.9 becomes 4 — a subtle source of small but systematic errors if rounding was actually intended.

questions.question: How would you convert a column of 'Yes'/'No' strings into actual boolean True/False values?
options: astype(bool) directly, which works automatically
Mapping the values explicitly, e.g. df['col'].map({'Yes': True, 'No': False})
This conversion isn't possible in pandas
Using pd.to_numeric()
questions.explanation: Explicitly mapping each string to its boolean equivalent avoids astype(bool)'s pitfall of treating any non-empty string as True.

questions.question: Why might leading zeros disappear from a product code column, like '007', if it's loaded as a numeric type?
options: Leading zeros are preserved automatically in every case
Numeric types don't preserve leading zeros, since 007 and 7 represent the same number
Pandas always keeps codes as text automatically
This only happens with negative numbers
questions.explanation: Because a numeric type only stores the numeric value, not its original text formatting, a code like '007' loaded as a number becomes 7, losing the leading zeros.

questions.question: How do you check the data type of every column in a DataFrame at once?
options: df.types
df.dtypes
df.check_types()
type(df)
questions.explanation: `.dtypes` returns the data type of each column in the DataFrame, letting you spot type mismatches quickly.

questions.question: Why do currency values like "$1,200" typically need string cleanup before converting to numeric?
options: They don't — pd.to_numeric() handles currency symbols automatically
The dollar sign and comma make the value a non-numeric string, so those characters must be stripped before conversion will succeed
Currency values can never be converted to numbers
Only negative currency values need cleanup
questions.explanation: Characters like $ and , aren't valid parts of a number, so they need to be removed (e.g. with .str.replace()) before pd.to_numeric() or astype(float) can parse the value.
